Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

amount noun

how much of something there is

also quantity, a large amount of

classical

Hor. S. 2.6.1: modus agrī nōn ita magnus
Cic. Att. 13.33.2: dē modō agrī (Lewis & Short)

modus, modī m.

noun, second declension

the amount, the measure of a thing

The measure of a thing: its size or quantity (Lewis & Short). In speech Latin more often asks quantum with a genitive: quantum operae, how much effort; tantum vīnī, so much wine.

Other words

  • vīs, vīs f. — a large amount, a mass (with a genitive)

    noun, third declension: accusative vim, ablative vī · also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 5.91: magna vīs aurī argentīque

  • quantitās, quantitātis f. — quantity, amount

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Plin. NH 17.219: quantitās ūmōris (Lewis & Short)

    Post-Augustan, and mostly technical: Vitruvius, the elder Pliny, Quintilian (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • hoc erat in vōtīs: modus agrī nōn ita magnus

    this is what I prayed for: an amount of land not so very bigHor. S. 2.6.1

  • Sōcratēs, in pompā cum magna vīs aurī argentīque ferrētur, «Quam multa nōn dēsīderō!» inquit.

    When a great amount of gold and silver was being carried in a procession, Socrates said: “How many things I don’t need!”Cic. Tusc. 5.91

  • sī, quantum operae sūmpsistī ut tuus pistor bonum faceret pānem, ejus duodecimam philosophiae dedissēs, ipse bonus jam prīdem essēs factus

    if you had given philosophy a twelfth of the amount of trouble you took to get your baker to make good bread, you would long ago have become good yourselfGell. 15.19.2, quoting Varro

See also a lot, amount, measure, size.
